PREAMBLE
Tan Sri Speaker Sir,
I beg to move that the Bill intituled “An Act to apply a sum from the
Consolidated Fund for service for the year 2027 and to appropriate
that sum for service for that year” be read a second time.
Bismillahirrahmanirrahim
Assalamualaikum Warahmatullahi Wabarakatuh,
Salam Sejahtera.
Tan Sri Speaker, Honourable Members of this House and my fellow
Malaysians, whom I hold dear,
1. Before I proceed, I extend my heartfelt thanks to everyone who
made the Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia 2026
such an orderly and resounding success. Beyond the F1 crews, the
event was carried by thousands of volunteers and civil servants. It
shows that when we join forces as one, in the spirit of segulai sejalai,

ews, the
event was carried by thousands of volunteers and civil servants. It
shows that when we join forces as one, in the spirit of segulai sejalai,
Malaysia can triumph on the world stage. So too at the 20th Asian
Games, where we matched our best-ever showing, with medallists
drawn from every race—proof that we are at our finest when we
draw strength from every community.
The nation is proud of you!
2. Every age gives a nation its own canvas on which to paint a
bolder, more inclusive landscape. Yet there are moments in the
folds of history when a nation is asked not merely to manage what
it has, but summoned to widen the horizon of its ambition, steel the
confidence of its people and shape the future together, with a clear
Budget Speech 2027 | 17

and profound grasp of the spirit of the age – the zeitgeist.
3. As Allah SWT reveals in Surah al-Hashr, verse 18:

O you who believe, be mindful of Allah, and let every soul look
to what it has sent ahead for tomorrow. And be mindful of Allah;
indeed, Allah is fully aware of all that you do.
4. The word lighad – “for tomorrow” – carries a demand both vast
and profound. No person, no community and no nation can live by
managing today alone. We are called to think ahead and to lay firm

a demand both vast
and profound. No person, no community and no nation can live by
managing today alone. We are called to think ahead and to lay firm
foundations for the future: to test those foundations, to ask which
doors we are opening or widening, and to weigh the legacy we will
leave to the generations to come.
5. True progress is measured not by how far we travel, but by what
we carry together along the way: human dignity, strong families,
a fair chance for each generation to rise, the integrity of our
institutions, and the conviction that effort will be repaid with
opportunity. It is not enough to inherit our strengths. We must
enlarge them, until they become a greater legacy for those
who follow.
6. The British philosopher and historian of ideas Sir Isaiah Berlin

s. We must
enlarge them, until they become a greater legacy for those
who follow.
6. The British philosopher and historian of ideas Sir Isaiah Berlin
borrowed an ancient image, simple yet sharp and profound: the
hedgehog and the fox. The fox knows many things; the hedgehog
knows one big thing. A nation needs both. A nation must hold
to one great and constant ambition: a purpose that gives the journey
18 | Budget Speech 2027

its direction and meaning. The economy demands growth and
distribution; technology, innovation and protection; public finances,
discipline and compassion; development, speed and wisdom.
A nation thus needs the hedgehog’s steadfastness of direction and
ambition, and the fox’s ingenuity in finding the paths and the means
to realise them.
7. The great Islamic thinker and jurist al-Mawardi, in his reflections
on the culture and conduct of government, held that power cannot
stand on its own without order, law and responsibility. Government
acquires meaning only when the trust of power is exercised justly,
when institutions function as they should, and when the interests
of the many are protected.
8. Today, that is our test. The world grows ever more turbulent.

titutions function as they should, and when the interests
of the many are protected.
8. Today, that is our test. The world grows ever more turbulent.
War, great-power rivalry and a disrupted climate are driving up the
price of food and the cost of energy. Supply chains we long took for
granted are fraying, testing the security of our food and our supplies.
Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping trade, energy, work and life
itself. Yet great change brings not only anxiety. It also opens doors
for nations bold enough to read the times, master new knowledge
and prepare their people early.
9. Malaysia must not merely weather change. We must have
the confidence to shape it. Before us lie the opportunities to leap
ahead in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, new energy, the

e. We must have
the confidence to shape it. Before us lie the opportunities to leap
ahead in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, new energy, the
digital economy and high-value industries; to raise productivity
and wages; to strengthen local enterprise; and to ensure that
young Malaysians are not mere consumers of change, but creators
of progress itself.
10. A truly successful economy, then, is not one that merely grows,
but one that answers to the lives of its people.
Budget Speech 2027 | 19

11. So our question is not simply how large an economy we wish
to build, but whether that growth opens room for families to save,
for workers to earn more dignified wages, for small businesses
to keep growing, and for every one of them to reach for the skies
while staying rooted to the ground.
12. And so let it be said plainly: a National Budget is a moral
statement, the National Covenant of a responsible Government.
13. Malay thought has long placed justice and trust at the very
heart and linchpin of government. The classical Malay poet and
historian Raja Ali Haji, in Gurindam Dua Belas (1847), wrote:
Hukum adil atas rakyat, (Just laws upon the people)
Tanda raja beroleh inayat. (Mark a ruler blessed with grace)
14. These terse lines carry a meaning that is vast and lasting: that

Tanda raja beroleh inayat. (Mark a ruler blessed with grace)
14. These terse lines carry a meaning that is vast and lasting: that
power is measured not by the grandeur of one’s station, but by
the justice the people can feel. Authority worthy of the name is not
merely strong. It knows that power must always walk hand in hand
with trust and accountability.
Raja mufakat dengan menteri, (A ruler in counsel with his ministers)
Seperti kebun berpagarkan duri. (Is a garden fenced with thorns)
15. In our tradition, the bond between those who govern and those
who are governed has never rested on power alone. It is anchored in
waad – a covenant, in which loyalty must be answered with justice,
and power must be fenced in by trust.
This is our National Covenant.

and power must be fenced in by trust.
This is our National Covenant.

16. That the nation will not abandon those crushed by hardship.
And that every Malaysian child, whatever their family, region or
station, has the right to see their potential, and to reach it.
17. Nor is this covenant one-sided. The nation provides the room
and the opportunity; the rakyat fill it with knowledge, work, creativity
and courage. The Government keeps its trust; the rakyat strengthen
the nation through effort and excellence.
It is a duty history has laid upon us.
18. Yet that duty is not a burden to be shouldered in gloom. It is
our generation’s chance to leave behind a nation stronger than the
one we inherited: with institutions more trusted, an economy more
diverse, and young people with greater room to forge their own
future.

ger than the
one we inherited: with institutions more trusted, an economy more
diverse, and young people with greater room to forge their own
future.
19. History is not carved by great names alone, but by the millions
who work every day: who teach and who heal, who trade and who
create, who till the soil, who care for their families and build their
lives.
20. The measure of a Budget, then, lies not in the thickness of its
pages, the size of its allocations or the number of its announcements.
The measure is far more fundamental: are more Malaysians able
to live with dignity, and will the Malaysia we hand to the next
generation be fairer than the one we inherited? If the answer is yes,
that is true progress. In the conviction that economic strength must,

the next
generation be fairer than the one we inherited? If the answer is yes,
that is true progress. In the conviction that economic strength must,
in the end, ennoble the human spirit; that growth must bear the fruit
of justice; that reform must restore trust; and that every generation
must bequeath a better nation than the last, I hereby present the
MADANI Budget 2027: a generation’s endeavour to strengthen the
nation’s order, and to keep our promise, our National Covenant, with
the future.
Budget Speech 2027 | 21

FOUR YEARS OF MADANI:
FROM STRUGGLE TO SUCCESS
21. Approaching its fourth year, the MADANI Government has set
the direction and policy framework of Ekonomi MADANI, followed by
bold reforms that are now bearing fruit.
● The Ekonomi MADANI Framework was introduced alongside
policies that drive growth and a fairer distribution of
wealth, such as the New Industrial Master Plan (NIMP) 2030,
the National Energy Transition Roadmap (NETR) and the
Bumiputera Economic Transformation Plan (PuTERA35).
● Only the MADANI Government has boldly ventured to reform
targeted subsidies. Subsidies are the rakyat’s privilege,
yet for years they bled out to foreign nationals and large
corporations. BUDI MADANI is a national success—targeting
subsidies to strengthen public finances while bringing prices

o foreign nationals and large
corporations. BUDI MADANI is a national success—targeting
subsidies to strengthen public finances while bringing prices
down for the rakyat. The result: subsidy money that once
leaked away now funds a near-doubling of assistance to the
rakyat, from 8 billion ringgit in 2022 to 15 billion ringgit under
STR and SARA this year. Imagine, too, had we kept putting off
subsidy targeting in the midst of this energy crisis: the fiscal
burden would have exceeded 40 billion ringgit.
● We have reinforced fiscal discipline. The Public Finance and
Fiscal Responsibility Act and the Government Procurement
Act were enacted to place the Finance Minister’s powers
under scrutiny. The Audit Act was expanded to track
and audit public money. The result: investor confidence

ed to place the Finance Minister’s powers
under scrutiny. The Audit Act was expanded to track
and audit public money. The result: investor confidence
has risen; growth has been strong and has beaten its
targets; investment and trade have reached record highs;
competitiveness has surged; and the Ringgit has been
Asia’s best performer.
22 | Budget Speech 2027

22. And so the Fifth MADANI Budget marks the next step towards
a great ambition for the face of Malaysia in the years ahead. As
reform presses on without fear, the fruits of growth, and every ringgit
saved through reform, must return to the rakyat as greater benefits.
23. In line with the Ekonomi MADANI Framework and the Thirteenth
to reach for the skies, while anchored to our values, built upon eight
principal Foundations. Today, I have chosen to present the broad
framework and the key announcements. For the rest, the full text
and its annexes, as circulated, are authoritative.
Budget Speech 2027 | 23

THRUST ONE
ADDRESSING THE COST OF LIVING FOR THE RAKYAT
24. The cost of living remains a pressing issue that weighs heavily
on the rakyat. Recognising this, the Government remains committed
to improving existing policies to ensure that the well-being of the
rakyat continues to be given priority.
● Last month, for instance, the Government provided further relief
to households by raising the electricity bill protection threshold
from 600 to 800 kWh per month. This adjustment benefits more
than 8 million domestic consumers, or up to 90 per cent of the
total.
● The Government also increased the monthly BUDI95 petrol
quota to 300 litres last month, while eligible jeep and pick-up
owners under BUDI Diesel were granted a quota of 400 litres

the monthly BUDI95 petrol
quota to 300 litres last month, while eligible jeep and pick-up
owners under BUDI Diesel were granted a quota of 400 litres
per month. September’s usage records show that only around
100 thousand users, or less than 1 per cent, reached their 300-litre
BUDI95 limit, while 15 thousand jeep and pick-up owners fully
utilised their 400-litre BUDI Diesel quota. These demonstrate that
the monthly quotas provided are sufficient to meet the needs of
the rakyat.
COST OF LIVING ASSISTANCE
25. The total provision for subsidies, assistance and incentives is
expected to exceed 80 billion ringgit next year. Of this amount, fuel
subsidies are expected to remain high at 40 billion ringgit, while
nearly 3.3 billion ringgit will be allocated for assistance through the

ount, fuel
subsidies are expected to remain high at 40 billion ringgit, while
nearly 3.3 billion ringgit will be allocated for assistance through the
Social Welfare Department (JKM).
24 | Budget Speech 2027

26. I am pleased to announce that the government will increase
the allocation for Sumbangan Tunai RAHMAH (STR) and Sumbangan
Asas RAHMAH (SARA) to 16 billion ringgit in 2027, compared with
15 billion ringgit previously.
● The government will extend SARA assistance of up to 150 ringgit
per month, or 1,800 ringgit annually, to all STR recipients, benefiting
up to 9 million Malaysians.
● In addition, the government will extend SARA MADANI assistance
of 100 ringgit, on two occasions, to Malaysians aged 18 and above
who are not STR recipients, with disbursements scheduled ahead of
Aidilfitri and in conjunction with the 70th National Day. This initiative
will benefit up to 13 million Malaysians, including those in the
M40 income group.

will benefit up to 13 million Malaysians, including those in the

● The Government has also agreed to extend the use of SARA to
purchases of fresh produce and perishable goods at 216 Farmers’
Markets and TAMU under Federal Agricultural Marketing Authority
(FAMA) nationwide.
● To date, the SARA programme has 15 thousand participating
business premises, including 6,800 small grocery shops and
cooperatives. The Government will widen the participation of small
grocery shops to 10 thousand by the end of this year.
27. Accordingly, the allocation for Jualan RAHMAH MADANI and
Jualan Agro MADANI will be increased from 630 million ringgit to 750
million ringgit, with a target of 35 thousand programmes nationwide.

● A total of 30 thousand Jualan RAHMAH programmes will be
organised across all State Legislative Assembly constituencies
(DUN). The Government will give greater attention to rural
Budget Speech 2027 | 25

communities, low-cost housing areas and urban Projek Perumahan
Rakyat (PPR), with efforts to increase the number of programmes
held in these locations. Distribution will also be broadened beyond
conventional grocery shops to include vending machines. At the
same time, Jualan RAHMAH MADANI Borong will be organised to
assist small traders.
● In addition, 5,000 Jualan Agro MADANI programmes will be
carried out, providing the public with access to fresh agricultural
produce such as fish, chicken, vegetables and fruit at prices up to
30 per cent lower.
28. The distribution of essential goods to rural and remote areas
will be expanded for the benefit of the rakyat, with an allocation of
250 million ringgit. This covers six new locations, including Kampung

income group, the M40, who continue to bear the burden of the cost
of living with patience and resilience. In this regard, I am pleased to
announce the following measures:
First: The individual tax relief for individual and
dependent relatives threshold, which was last reviewed in 2010,
will be raised from 9,000 ringgit to 12,000 ringgit.
Second: The income tax rates for resident individuals will be
reduced by one percentage point.

reduced by one percentage point.
● For chargeable income band ranging from
70,001 ringgit to 100,000 ringgit, the rate will be
reduced to 18 per cent.

● Care of parents and grandparents will cover all

well as pet vaccination expenses and the cost of

30. At the same time, the Government remains committed
to progressive taxation. Accordingly, the tax rate applicable to
high-income earners with income exceeding 1 million ringgit will be
adjusted to 30 per cent.
31. Collectively, the increase in tax relief and reduction in
individual income tax rates will provide approximately 5 million
taxpayers with additional disposable income of up to 1,600 ringgit.
DECENT WAGES FOR THE RAKYAT
32. Narrowing the gap between productivity and workers’ wages
must remain a priority. The pressure on the cost of living becomes
an increasingly heavy burden when income growth fails to keep
Budget Speech 2027 | 27

pace with increases in the prices of goods. This concern is reflected
in Malaysia’s labour compensation share of GDP, which remains
relatively low at 33.9 per cent.
● The Government has decided to raise the minimum wage from
1,700 ringgit to 2,000 ringgit. The new rate will take effect from
June 2027, benefiting more than 4 million workers. MSMEs with
annual sales below 50 million ringgit will be exempted to provide
room for adjustment to business models.
● We acknowledge that the minimum wage provides a necessary
floor for workers’ incomes, but it does not address the wider
issue of wages that do not adequately reflect the skills and
qualifications of our workforce. Accordingly, the MADANI
government will reform the workers’ income framework,

not adequately reflect the skills and
qualifications of our workforce. Accordingly, the MADANI
government will reform the workers’ income framework,
beginning with a minimum wage of 2,500 ringgit a month for
semi-skilled workers and graduates.
● The Government also welcomes the commitment by
Government-Linked Investment Companies (GLICs) and
Government-Linked Companies (GLCs) to raise the living wage
benchmark from 3,100 ringgit to 3,400 ringgit per month. This
initiative is expected to benefit 230 thousand workers.
● The Government has raised the minimum wage, introduced a
minimum wage for semi-skilled workers and graduates, and
increased civil servants’ salaries. GLICs and GLCs have also set
the example. Several employers in key sectors, including banking

and graduates, and
increased civil servants’ salaries. GLICs and GLCs have also set

as well as oil and gas, have likewise established more decent
wage levels. In this regard, I urge all private-sector employers
to follow suit and play their part in ensuring that workers receive
fairer remuneration.
28 | Budget Speech 2027

33. In relation to wages, the Government will make further efforts
to curb the employment of undocumented foreign workers.
Companies other than MSMEs may claim tax deductions on salary
expenses only if salary are paid through bank account or cashless
payment instruments permitted under the Employment Act 1955.
Tax deduction for other expenses will not be subject to this
requirement.
RIGHTS OF GIG WORKERS
34. An estimated 600 thousand Malaysians make their living as
e-hailing and p-hailing drivers. The MADANI Government will pursue
a more comprehensive approach to the protection of gig workers.
● The Gig Workers Consultative Council is currently negotiating
to establish a minimum income rate, a formula for determining
income and minimum standards of social protection for gig workers.

urrently negotiating
to establish a minimum income rate, a formula for determining
income and minimum standards of social protection for gig workers.
The process is expected to be finalised in early 2027.
● Pending the finalisation of this process, the Government and
Grab Holdings Limited have agreed to share the cost of a 160 million
ringgit package, to be implemented beginning 2027. This initiative
is intended to enhance the net income and strengthen measures to
safeguard the welfare of e-hailing and p-hailing workers.
● This package will include an increase in the minimum income

PREFACE
The global economy is entering 2027 amid
profound change. Geopolitical tensions are
reshaping trade, investment and energy
security. Climate risks are becoming more
immediate, while technological advances
are transforming industries, jobs and the
foundations of competitiveness. These
forces are increasingly interconnected,
creating both new challenges and new
opportunities for Malaysia.
The experience of recent years has
demonstrated the importance of
resilience and adaptability. The pandemic,
disruptions to global supply chains,
heightened geopolitical tensions and rapid
technological change have altered the
environment in which economic policy
is made. Malaysia must respond not by
seeking a return to old assumptions, but
by preparing confidently for the world now
emerging.

economic outlook 2027 iii

The results thus far have been encouraging. Economic growth exceeded expectations in
both 2024 and 2025. This momentum continued into 2026, with the economy expanding
by 5.7% in the first half of the year. Full-year growth is now expected to be at the upper
end of the projected range of 4.8% to 5.3%.
Yet headline growth cannot be the sole measure of our progress. The greater imperative
is to translate stronger investment and economic expansion into higher incomes, better
jobs and wider opportunities for Malaysians, particularly our youth. Investments secured
today must strengthen productive capacity, deepen domestic capabilities and create high-
value opportunities for the future.
Our approach is grounded in sound economic principles and empirical evidence, but

Our approach is grounded in sound economic principles and empirical evidence, but
policy cannot be shaped by models and statistics alone. It must also respond to the lived
realities of the rakyat, their aspirations, anxieties and experiences of the economy in
their daily lives.
Raising the Ceiling of Malaysia’s economic potential must ultimately serve to Raise the
Floor of the rakyat’s living standards. Both must rest on the firm foundation of good
governance.
Progress cannot be judged by economic statistics alone if its benefits are not broadly
shared. Fiscal reforms have enabled the Government to direct resources more effectively
towards those who need them. Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah, Sumbangan Asas Rahmah and

forms have enabled the Government to direct resources more effectively
towards those who need them. Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah, Sumbangan Asas Rahmah and
BUDI MADANI continue to provide essential support to households, particularly as global
energy prices and supply disruptions place renewed pressure on the cost of living.
Social protection, however, cannot substitute for productive opportunity. Our
responsibility is to provide security and assistance where they are needed today, while
creating the conditions for higher incomes, better employment and greater social
mobility tomorrow.

position in more than a decade. This progress reflects the strength of our economic

There remains much more to do. Malaysia must move decisively towards higher-value
manufacturing, accelerate the energy transition and strengthen its capabilities in artificial
intelligence, robotics and other emerging technologies. These are among the forces
reshaping global investment, productivity and competitiveness.

iv economic outlook 2027

These efforts are expected to support economic growth of between 4.2% and 5.2% in
2027. The significance of this outlook, however, lies not only in the headline number. It
lies in whether growth delivers stronger productivity, better wages, quality employment
and a more secure future for Malaysians.
The year ahead will remain challenging. Geopolitical fragmentation, climate risks and
rapid technological change will continue to reshape the global economic landscape.
Malaysia must therefore remain agile, strengthen its resilience and pursue reform with
clarity and purpose.
Our task is not to recreate the economy of the past, but to build one capable of
succeeding in the world now emerging — an economy that is more productive and
competitive, yet also more inclusive, sustainable and humane.

Malaysia's Journey in Financing for Sustainability
Malaysia has always been at the forefront of laying the foundations for financing sustainability through national environmental, energy
and climate policies, complemented by fiscal incentives to encourage green investments. Commencing 2014 onwards, efforts have
been intensified towards developing the regulatory frameworks, financial instruments and market infrastructure needed to mobilise
public and private capital to support the country's sustainability goals including climate initiatives. The highlights are as follows:

Lifting Wages from the Ground Up
In collaboration with THE FUTURE1
Introduction
Malaysia has made significant progress in strengthening the wage ecosystem and improving
workers’ living standards through various decent wage policies. These initiatives have successfully
raised the wage floor for low-paid workers, strengthened income progression and established
important foundations for a more inclusive and productive labour market. As the market becomes
more dynamic, the next policy challenge lies in ensuring workers are able to progress more
meaningfully beyond the wage floor throughout the career path.
The challenge facing Malaysia’s wage ecosystem is deeply rooted in the structure of its economy,

ly beyond the wage floor throughout the career path.
The challenge facing Malaysia’s wage ecosystem is deeply rooted in the structure of its economy,
particularly the concentration of labour-intensive micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in
persistently low-wage industries. While existing policies have strengthened wage protection and
workers capabilities, further uplift towards sustainable wage growth requires firms to generate
greater demand for high-skilled workers and better-paying jobs. This article analyses the current
structural wage imbalances and proposes policy options needed for a targeted 'big push' that
integrates MSMEs’ upgrading, industrial development and workforce interventions. By positioning

policy options needed for a targeted 'big push' that
integrates MSMEs’ upgrading, industrial development and workforce interventions. By positioning
productivity as the bridge between stronger business capabilities and wage progression, the
country will be able to address structural wage imbalances, strengthen the wage ladder and ensure
economic growth delivers broader improvements in workers’ living standards.
From a Higher Wage Floor to a Stronger Wage Ladder
Over the years, Malaysia’s economic expansion has generated employment and raised nominal
wages, but the distribution of these gains across workers remains uneven. An important indicator
of economic growth distributed to workers is the labour income share, measured by compensation

across workers remains uneven. An important indicator
of economic growth distributed to workers is the labour income share, measured by compensation
of employees (CE). A rising labour income share suggests that workers are benefitting more from
the gains in production, whereas a persistently low or declining share may indicate that economic
growth is not being translated proportionately into employee compensation.
As shown in Figure 1.1.1., the CE accounted for 33.6% of Malaysia’s GDP in 2024, which remained
below the pre COVID-19 pandemic levels. Although GDP and employment have recovered, the post-
pandemic pattern highlights a continuing challenge in ensuring economic recovery translates into
broad-based improvements in labour income. This situation points to an important dimension in

challenge in ensuring economic recovery translates into
broad-based improvements in labour income. This situation points to an important dimension in
Malaysia’s wage challenge, as the issue extends beyond the earnings of low-paid workers to the
capacity of the economic structure in generating sustained and widely shared wage progression.
To understand the overall wage dynamics, it is important to distinguish the varying impacts of the
minimum wage policy, the compression of wages and the disproportionate wage growth.

distribution moved from below RM1,300 in 2015 to approximately RM1,700 — RM2,000 in 2024.
This pattern is consistent with minimum wage adjustments lifting the lower tail of the distribution
and reducing the concentration of workers in the lowest wage brackets.

Nevertheless, a substantial proportion of wage recipients continues to earn close to the statutory
minimum, while the middle-wage bracket remains comparatively narrow. This reflects the different
wage dynamics across the distribution, as the statutory minimum wage directly lifts wages at the
lower end, while workers in the higher brackets above the minimum wage are not necessarily
offered wage adjustments. The lack of wage adjustments assurance would result in relatively
weaker wage progression within the middle-wage bracket. While wage spillover effects remain
limited, the minimum wage has been more effective as a protective floor than as a mechanism for
generating sustained wage progression beyond the floor.

Figure 1.1.2. also shows that the actual wage distribution in Malaysia is skewed to the right, where
the majority of workers earn relatively modest wages, while a small proportion of high-income
earners receive substantially larger wages. This scenario presents a wider gap compared to the
ideal distribution, which depicts the broad characteristics of a more mature high-wage economy.
Moving towards the ideal distribution requires more than periodic adjustments to the statutory
minimum wage, alongside stronger productivity growth, occupational upgrading and the creation of
more middle- and high-skilled jobs.

The Missing Middle is Concentrated among Semi-Skilled Workers
Although skills command a wage premium, employment remains concentrated in semi-skilled
occupations, reflecting the underlying structure of the economy. As shown in Figure 1.1.3., semi-
skilled occupations accounted for 55.4% of total employment in 2024, compared with 36.5% for
skilled and 8.1% for low-skilled. Consequently, the wage distribution is shaped principally by the
earnings trajectory of semi-skilled workers, rather than by low-skilled employment alone.

or supply-side objectives. It must be complemented by demand-side initiatives that promote firm
and industrial upgrading through automation and digitalisation, with productivity serving as the
critical link between higher-value economic activities and sustainable wage progression. The key
challenge is to ensure that wage increases are underpinned by productivity improvements that
make such progression sustainable over time for the labour market to reach an ideal state, where

The simulated productivity-wage alignment in Figure 1.1.9. highlights a fundamental condition for
sustainable wage progression where real wage needs to grow in tandem with productivity over the
medium to longer term. Raising wages must correspond with productivity gains to avoid widening
the gap between labour costs and productive capacity, as this would affect a firm’s competitiveness
and employment decisions. On the other hand, the labour income share would weaken if workers’
productivity improvements are not adequately compensated through higher wages, resulting in
constrained domestic demand. A sustainable high-wage economy therefore requires productivity

Nevertheless, the central challenge in the labour market that impedes the intended outcome lies
in the limited integration between the supply and demand for skills. While education and training
institutions shape the supply of workforce, the types of skills, occupations and jobs demanded
by the economy are determined by the industry. When these two sides are insufficiently aligned,
the labour market may experience persistent skills mismatches, youth unemployment and
underemployment, weak wage progression and a disconnect between productivity and wages.

These indicate that improvements in education and training alone may not translate into better
wage outcomes unless firms simultaneously create high-paying jobs and strengthen demand for
more advanced skills.
Way Forward
Malaysia’s next phase of wage reform should move beyond raising the wage floor towards building
a stronger wage ladder that enables meaningful career progression for workers. While maintaining
an effective national minimum wage remains important for protecting workers at the lower end
of the labour market, wage regulation alone would not transform the underlying structure of

simultaneously strengthens workers’ opportunities to move up the wage ladder and firms’ capacity
to support higher wages through productivity growth and higher-value economic activities. This is
particularly important given the continued concentration of employment in labour-intensive and
relatively low-wage industries.

The Role of Government Measures in Cushioning Rising Living Costs
Introduction
As a small and open economy, Malaysia is exposed to heightened global uncertainties, including
volatility in global energy prices. Focusing on the price transmission channel, any disruption could
raise import and production costs, exert upward pressure on consumer prices and, in turn, weigh
on business activities and household spending. Nonetheless, Malaysia’s position as a net energy
exporter provides buffers against the impact in the domestic market. Against this backdrop, this
article examines:
• the impact of higher global oil prices on producer and consumer prices;

and transport-related services that rely on energy and imported inputs. Given the role of Brent

Government Measures to Cushion the Impact of Rising Living Costs
The Government has adopted a broad and complementary set of measures to cushion the impact
of rising living costs and safeguard household wellbeing, particularly during periods of heightened
external cost pressures. These measures operate through two main channels: price stabilisation
measures which help moderate increases in the price of essential goods and services; and
targeted assistance which provides direct financial support to improve the remaining income1 of

eligible households and vulnerable groups. Together, these interventions help preserve households’
purchasing power by addressing both the increase in expenditure and strengthening the financial
capacity to absorb higher living costs.

the transmission of higher global energy prices to the costs of domestic essential items, as
shown in Figure 1.2.4. This is particularly important for lower-income households, which have
smaller income buffers and less capacity to absorb increases in essential expenditure. The price

heterogeneous across households, the household-level microsimulation indicates that Government

highlight the complementary nature of the Government’s policy response in safeguarding the
livelihoods of households, particularly during periods of elevated cost pressures. Price stabilisation
measures help contain the increase in household expenditure through the price channel, while

The energy sector is undergoing a significant transformation as countries seek to reduce their
reliance on fossil fuels and accelerate the adoption of cleaner sources of electricity. Electricity
demand is increasing rapidly driven by the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI), data centres,
electric vehicles (EVs) and the electrification of industries traditionally dependent on fossil fuels.
The scale of this transformation is particularly evident in Southeast Asia. According to the
International Energy Agency (IEA), regional electricity demand increased by more than 7% in 2024,
which is nearly twice the global average. Under the IEA’s current-policies scenario, electricity

From Vision to Reality
The APG is based on a simple idea that AMS can benefit by connecting their electricity systems.
At present, AMS largely manage their electricity systems at the domestic level. However, demand
and supply do not always move in the same direction. One economy may have excess electricity
while another is facing a shortage. Cross-border connections can help balance these differences.

AMS do not operate under one common electricity law or regulatory system. Each AMS retains
authority over its own electricity sector including generation, transmission, distribution, licensing,
electricity pricing, market access and system operation. This means that the legal rules governing
cross-border electricity trade can differ significantly from one economy to another. The APG

Strengthening Grid Resilience
While regional electricity trade under the APG enhances Malaysia’s ability to manage rising
electricity demand, the increasing interconnectedness of power systems also makes grid resilience
a critical priority. Malaysia therefore needs to maintain adequate domestic generation capacity,
robust transmission infrastructure and diversified supply routes to ensure that disruptions,
congestion or failures along any single corridor do not cascade across the wider system. A resilient
grid will allow Malaysia to manage fluctuations in RE generation and cross-border power flows
more effectively, while supporting reliable participation in regional electricity trading without

Conclusion
The ASEAN Power Grid is expected to become the regional electricity network by 2045, allowing
AMS to trade electricity seamlessly and increase the use of RE. The APG is also expected to shift
from a mainly bilateral to multilateral electricity trading arrangement, allowing economies with
excess electricity to supply to other AMS in need. Malaysia’s strategic geographical position, well-
developed power infrastructure and resilient financial framework are uniquely suited to capitalise

Malaysia’s strategic geographical position, well-
developed power infrastructure and resilient financial framework are uniquely suited to capitalise
on regional energy grid integration. However, challenges such as regulatory disharmonisation
and grid flexibility need to be managed. Sustained investments in energy storage, transmission
networks, grid technology, and renewable power remain essential to achieve APG goals. Beyond
boosting economic growth and reinforcing ASEAN’s energy security, the APG offers Malaysia a vital
opportunity to solidify its position in the regional energy market.

Tourism generates economic value through foreign and domestic spending, creates jobs, provides
opportunities for local businesses as well as communities and improves public infrastructure.
According to the World Bank (2026), the arrival of visitors for business or leisure purposes is a
powerful economic driver for the national growth and livelihoods particularly in developing and
middle-income economies. The World Tourism Barometer report by UN Tourism in September 2026

stated that international tourist arrivals grew by 4.7% in 2025, with an estimated 1.5 billion arrivals

receipts increased by 7.8%, reaching around USD1.9 trillion, reflecting robust global travel demand
and higher visitor spending. The continued expansion of international tourism underscores the
industry’s significant contribution to global economic activity, employment, trade and services.

Multiplier Effects of Inbound Tourism
An assessment by the Ministry of Finance indicates that inbound tourism expenditure generates
spillovers across a broad range of industries. Inbound visitors spending of RM10 billion will result
in an additional RM6.8 billion gross output to the economy. The total gross output is estimated
at RM16.8 billion, generated across 27 industries, representing an output multiplier of 1.68 times.
Primary tourism-facing industries generate the highest output totalling RM11.4 billion, mainly in
the transportation and storage, restaurants, accommodation as well as wholesale and retail trade
as illustrated in Figure 3.1.9. Meanwhile, nearly a third of the economic impact is contributed

, accommodation as well as wholesale and retail trade

by indirect and supporting industries including agriculture and manufacturing. The broad-based
spillovers underscore the importance of maximising value capture from higher visitor arrivals,
particularly by increasing spending and length of stay. The impact extends beyond tourism-facing
industries through supply chain linkages, benefitting economic activity, employment, household
incomes and services exports. Maximising this impact requires enhancing connectivity; improving
tourism infrastructure, strengthening supply chain linkages and integrating local businesses directly

Navigating Headwinds
While increasing overall arrival numbers remains essential, relying solely on volume exposes
Malaysia to strategic vulnerabilities, requiring a concerted effort to address key operational
and market challenges. Geographically, heavy source-market concentration leaves the industry
vulnerable to localised economic shocks, while intense competition from neighbouring destinations
necessitates continuous product diversification. Accessibility remains constrained by limited direct
flights, volatile jet fuel prices, high airfares and airspace rerouting due to geopolitical tensions.

Introduction
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important energy chokepoints, while the
Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Suez Canal form part of a major trade corridor between Asia
and Europe. The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, serves as a key
gateway connecting the Middle East with global markets and facilitating oil and gas exports.
Meanwhile, Bab el-Mandeb Strait, connects the Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea, which leads to
the Mediterranean Sea via Suez Canal.

This article examines how geopolitical shocks can affect Malaysia’s manufacturing sector through
energy markets, maritime logistics and global supply chains. It combines industry evidence with
input-output (IO) analysis to identify sectoral exposure, estimate the potential impact on production
costs and assess which industries could transmit shocks more widely across the economy.
Manufacturing Performance and External Exposure
Despite the latest episode of geopolitical uncertainty, Malaysia’s manufacturing sector remained
robust supported by sustained production and strong external demand. Manufacturing value-
added expanded by 6.6% in the first half of 2026, underpinned by stronger activity in E&E as well

on and strong external demand. Manufacturing value-

as petroleum, chemical, rubber and plastic products subsectors. This performance is aligned with
total trade which increased by 22.4% to RM1,795.2 billion, supported by higher exports (27.5%)
and imports (16.8%). These developments indicate sustained external demand for Malaysia’s
manufactured products.
However, the sources of growth and external exposure varied between export- and domestic-
oriented industries. Export-oriented industries particularly E&E as well as petroleum and chemical
products, continued to drive growth, supported by sustained external demand. The E&E industry

ries particularly E&E as well as petroleum and chemical
products, continued to drive growth, supported by sustained external demand. The E&E industry
benefited from continued investment in artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology-intensive
activities which support demand for semiconductors and electronic components. Nevertheless,
export-oriented industries could still be affected by demand and shipping disruptions. Meanwhile,
domestic-oriented industries, including food processing, fabricated metal products and transport

The impact of these risks on production depends on a firm’s sourcing flexibility, inventory

ecosystem.

Government Responses
In light of the heightened tensions, the Government reactivated the National Economic Action
Council (MTEN) in March 2026, to coordinate a whole-of-government response to the economic
repercussions and global supply chain disruptions. The Government’s immediate response focused
on sustaining business liquidity and securing essential supplies. Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM)
introduced the RM5 billion SME Stabilisation Relief Facility to provide working capital financing to
viable SMEs affected by the West Asia conflict. As of August 2026, approximately RM2.8 billion was
approved to more than 4,900 SME accounts. More targeted assistance was provided through an

nflict. As of August 2026, approximately RM2.8 billion was

additional RM5 billion guarantee facility under Syarikat Jaminan Pembiayaan Perniagaan (SJPP) with
financing coverage to 80% and the guarantee tenure extended to 10 years for micro, small and
medium enterprises affected by the West Asia conflict. The facility was further complemented by
the broader RM10 billion BNM–CGC Guarantee Scheme, to support SMEs productivity, innovation
and resilience.

Way Forward
While the Government’s responses helped address immediate financing and supply pressures, a
more systematic approach is required to identify critical inputs, monitor concentrated supply risks
and coordinate early intervention. The immediate priority is to enhance visibility over critical inputs
and concentrated sources of supply. A targeted supply chain mapping programme should identify

and concentrated sources of supply. A targeted supply chain mapping programme should identify
common upstream suppliers, source country concentration, inventory coverage, lead times and
the availability of technically acceptable substitutes. The programme should focus on industries
with both extensive production linkages and high exposure, including refined petroleum, basic
chemicals, electronic components and selected machinery industries. A shared risk dashboard could
then support early warning signals and a more timely coordination and necessary action to be
taken by government agencies as well as the industries.
Further policy measures should facilitate alternative sourcing as preparation for potential disruption

government agencies as well as the industries.
Further policy measures should facilitate alternative sourcing as preparation for potential disruption
arising from any crises. This includes pre-qualifying substitute suppliers and materials, accelerating
technical approvals where safety and quality requirements are met, and utilising regional supplier-
matching platforms. For critical inputs with limited substitutes and high disruption costs, firms
should be encouraged to establish appropriate inventory buffers and strategic business viability.
Simultaneously, public support should be targeted, finite and conditional to limit costs as well as
minimise distortions.

Anchoring Malaysia’s Momentum Through GEAR-uP
In 2024, the Ministry of Finance (MoF) initiated the Government-Linked Enterprises Activation
and Reform Programme (GEAR-uP) to strengthen strategic investments, innovation and social
inclusion in supporting the nation’s economic development agenda. The Programme mobilises
six government-linked investment companies (GLICs), namely Employees Provident Fund (EPF),
Permodalan Nasional Berhad (PNB), Retirement Fund (Incorporated) (KWAP), Khazanah Nasional
Berhad (Khazanah), Lembaga Tabung Haji (Tabung Haji) and Lembaga Tabung Angkatan Tentera

B), Retirement Fund (Incorporated) (KWAP), Khazanah Nasional
Berhad (Khazanah), Lembaga Tabung Haji (Tabung Haji) and Lembaga Tabung Angkatan Tentera
(LTAT), together with the government-linked companies (GLCs) under their ownership. The initiatives
under these GLICs are aligned with the twin pillars of Ekonomi MADANI, namely Raising the Ceiling
of national potential and Raising the Floor of living standards. The six GLICs collectively manage
RM2.2 trillion in assets under management, exceeding Malaysia’s GDP in 2025.

into the first quarter of 2026. This is patient capital intended to crowd in private investments and

GLICs actively steward the portfolio of 37 GLCs, targeting 7.5% annualised total shareholder returns
from 2024 to 2028, a trajectory that could unlock RM100 billion in value. Performance has outpaced
expectations, with GLICs delivering total shareholder returns of 8% for full year 2025. As GLCs
account for around 27% of market capitalisation on Bursa Malaysia’s MAIN Market, the gains flow
back to EPF, KWAP, PNB and Tabung Haji members, lifting ordinary Malaysians’ savings.
This stewardship rests on clear targets benchmarked against best-in-class sector peers, comprising

Key Capital Market Measures
Several key measures were undertaken by the Securities Commission Malaysia (SC) and Bursa Malaysia in the first eight months of 2026 to
enhance the liquidity and efficiency of Malaysia’s capital market as follows:
Bursa Malaysia's First Financial Performance-based Indexes to
1
Strengthen Quality-driven Investing 12 JAN
The Bursa Malaysia Quality 50 Index (BMQ) and Bursa Malaysia Quality 50 Shariah Index (BMQ-S) are Bursa Malaysia's first financial
performance-based indexes, designed to elevate the visibility of resilient local enterprises. The new benchmarks identify 50 financially resilient Main

rformance-based indexes, designed to elevate the visibility of resilient local enterprises. The new benchmarks identify 50 financially resilient Main
and ACE Market companies outside the FTSE Bursa Malaysia Kuala Lumpur Composite Index (FBM KLCI) based on profitability, capital structure and
earnings quality, providing investors with a standardised tool to identify fundamentally strong companies. The indexes broaden access to quality
investment opportunities, strengthen investor confidence and support a more vibrant Malaysian equity market.
Malaysia's First Social Exchange to Strengthen Access to
2
12 FEB Social Impact Financing
Malaysia’s first Social Exchange platform, Impakrintas, operational since 19 February 2026, provides a regulated and transparent avenue for non-profit

alaysia’s first Social Exchange platform, Impakrintas, operational since 19 February 2026, provides a regulated and transparent avenue for non-profit
organisations (NPOs) to raise donations for eligible social impact projects while giving donors greater visibility over their contributions. The Government
allocated a RM2 million grant, administered by the SC, to partially defray eligible NPOs’ onboarding and fundraising costs, while donations through the
platform qualify for tax treatment under the Income Tax Act 1967. The platform strengthens public-private collaboration in social impact financing. It will
progressively expand to include social enterprises, community-based initiatives and other market-based avenues that support social and
climate-resilient outcomes.

3
Capital Market Transformation 9 MAR
The Capital Market Masterplan 2026 – 2030 (CMP) sets out Malaysia's five-year strategy to expand the capital market to between RM5.8 trillion –
RM6.3 trillion by 2030 while strengthening the country's global leadership in Islamic finance through Maqasid al-Shariah-driven innovations. The
Masterplan introduces 56 strategic initiatives to enhance market vibrancy, broaden access to capital, increase investment opportunities, accelerate

e
Masterplan introduces 56 strategic initiatives to enhance market vibrancy, broaden access to capital, increase investment opportunities, accelerate
sustainable and Islamic finance as well as strengthen regional market connectivity. Aligned with the Ekonomi MADANI framework, the CMP is projected
to elevate the capital market at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6% – 8%, optimising market valuations and mobilising climate transition
financing while broadening public access to wealth creation.
MyCIF's Silver Economy Scheme and VC-led Profit-Sharing
4
16 MAR Incentive to Improve MSME Funding Access
The Malaysia Co-Investment Fund (MyCIF), administered by the SC, has launched two landmark funding initiatives allocating RM50 million to accelerate

The Malaysia Co-Investment Fund (MyCIF), administered by the SC, has launched two landmark funding initiatives allocating RM50 million to accelerate
MSME growth. MyCIF introduced the Silver Economy Scheme to channel alternative financing focusing in care-tech, specialised healthcare and senior
living solutions. Furthermore, under the VC/PE Profit-Sharing Incentive, MyCIF will share 50% of exit profits with venture capital (VC) and private equity
(PE) firms that lead deals on regulated equity crowdfunding (ECF) platforms, bridging critical early-stage financing gaps while building a robust
wealth-creation pipeline aligned with the Ekonomi MADANI framework.

Islamic Capital Market Innovation 26 MAR
The SC established the Islamic Capital Market (ICM) Innovation Lab (FIKRALab) under the CMP as a structured co-creation and applied R&D platform
to develop new ICM products and instruments. Anchored on Maqasid al-Shariah as well as guided by halal and toyyib principles, FIKRALab expands
beyond fintech-centric ICM innovation by enabling deeper collaboration between the SC and industry in ideation, research, product design and pilot
testing. Key features include Maqasid al-Shariah clinics to assess and enhance existing ICM products and to reinforce real economy linkages,

nd pilot

beginning with a pilot project to develop an innovative instrument to unlock shariah-derived income within mixed activity groups. The first FIKRALab
cohort is expected to commence in Q4 2026, focusing on new generation ICM products and services, Islamic social finance and social capital as well
as sustainability and transition finance.

Bursa Malaysia and Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) signed an MoU to deepen regional market connectivity, with the HKEX Bursa
Malaysia Large Cap Index introduced as the first outcome of the partnership. The index tracks 60 leading listed companies across both markets,
comprising 30 constituents from each market with index weightings of approximately 40% for Malaysia and 60% for Hong Kong. It provides investors with
a new cross-market benchmark and supports future exchange traded fund (ETF) products. The partnership opens opportunities for collaboration in dual
listings, shariah-compliant products and carbon markets thus enhancing Malaysia's international market profile.

Bursa Malaysia officially implemented an equities trading data reclassification on 6 April 2026 to provide greater transparency and highly granular insights
into retail and institutional fund flows. Under this new reporting framework, nominee accounts are now accurately categorised at the trade level based on
end-beneficiary information rather than lumped into institutional data. On the other hand, foreign-owned institutions incorporated in Malaysia are refined
by fund origin to better reflect true market activity. The structural update does not alter total daily trading values. This reclassification will provide investors

Under the CMP, the Equity Guidelines was revised to strengthen the public market framework by enhancing the distinct roles of the Main Market and ACE
Market. The framework raises the Main Market's profit admission requirements, financial reporting standards, flexibility in assessing operating cash flow
and broader eligibility for infrastructure-type listings. Meanwhile, the ACE Market is reinforced as a sponsor-driven platform for growth companies with
enhanced listing requirements, including a minimum of two years post-listing track record prior to transfer to the Main Market. The reforms strengthen
listing quality, improve investor protection and support companies at different stages of growth.

Lifting Wages from the Ground Up
In collaboration with THE FUTURE1
Introduction
Malaysia has made significant progress in strengthening the wage ecosystem and improving
workers’ living standards through various decent wage policies. These initiatives have successfully
raised the wage floor for low-paid workers, strengthened income progression and established
important foundations for a more inclusive and productive labour market. As the market becomes
more dynamic, the next policy challenge lies in ensuring workers are able to progress more
meaningfully beyond the wage floor throughout the career path.
The challenge facing Malaysia’s wage ecosystem is deeply rooted in the structure of its economy,

ly beyond the wage floor throughout the career path.
The challenge facing Malaysia’s wage ecosystem is deeply rooted in the structure of its economy,
particularly the concentration of labour-intensive micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in
persistently low-wage industries. While existing policies have strengthened wage protection and
workers capabilities, further uplift towards sustainable wage growth requires firms to generate
greater demand for high-skilled workers and better-paying jobs. This article analyses the current
structural wage imbalances and proposes policy options needed for a targeted 'big push' that
integrates MSMEs’ upgrading, industrial development and workforce interventions. By positioning

policy options needed for a targeted 'big push' that
integrates MSMEs’ upgrading, industrial development and workforce interventions. By positioning
productivity as the bridge between stronger business capabilities and wage progression, the
country will be able to address structural wage imbalances, strengthen the wage ladder and ensure
economic growth delivers broader improvements in workers’ living standards.
From a Higher Wage Floor to a Stronger Wage Ladder
Over the years, Malaysia’s economic expansion has generated employment and raised nominal
wages, but the distribution of these gains across workers remains uneven. An important indicator
of economic growth distributed to workers is the labour income share, measured by compensation

across workers remains uneven. An important indicator
of economic growth distributed to workers is the labour income share, measured by compensation
of employees (CE). A rising labour income share suggests that workers are benefitting more from
the gains in production, whereas a persistently low or declining share may indicate that economic
growth is not being translated proportionately into employee compensation.
As shown in Figure 1.1.1., the CE accounted for 33.6% of Malaysia’s GDP in 2024, which remained
below the pre COVID-19 pandemic levels. Although GDP and employment have recovered, the post-
pandemic pattern highlights a continuing challenge in ensuring economic recovery translates into
broad-based improvements in labour income. This situation points to an important dimension in

challenge in ensuring economic recovery translates into
broad-based improvements in labour income. This situation points to an important dimension in
Malaysia’s wage challenge, as the issue extends beyond the earnings of low-paid workers to the
capacity of the economic structure in generating sustained and widely shared wage progression.
To understand the overall wage dynamics, it is important to distinguish the varying impacts of the
minimum wage policy, the compression of wages and the disproportionate wage growth.

This pattern is consistent with minimum wage adjustments lifting the lower tail of the distribution

Nevertheless, a substantial proportion of wage recipients continues to earn close to the statutory
minimum, while the middle-wage bracket remains comparatively narrow. This reflects the different
wage dynamics across the distribution, as the statutory minimum wage directly lifts wages at the
lower end, while workers in the higher brackets above the minimum wage are not necessarily
offered wage adjustments. The lack of wage adjustments assurance would result in relatively
weaker wage progression within the middle-wage bracket. While wage spillover effects remain
limited, the minimum wage has been more effective as a protective floor than as a mechanism for
generating sustained wage progression beyond the floor.

earners receive substantially larger wages. This scenario presents a wider gap compared to the
ideal distribution, which depicts the broad characteristics of a more mature high-wage economy.
Moving towards the ideal distribution requires more than periodic adjustments to the statutory
minimum wage, alongside stronger productivity growth, occupational upgrading and the creation of
more middle- and high-skilled jobs.

or supply-side objectives. It must be complemented by demand-side initiatives that promote firm
and industrial upgrading through automation and digitalisation, with productivity serving as the
critical link between higher-value economic activities and sustainable wage progression. The key
challenge is to ensure that wage increases are underpinned by productivity improvements that
make such progression sustainable over time for the labour market to reach an ideal state, where

sustainable wage progression where real wage needs to grow in tandem with productivity over the
medium to longer term. Raising wages must correspond with productivity gains to avoid widening
the gap between labour costs and productive capacity, as this would affect a firm’s competitiveness
and employment decisions. On the other hand, the labour income share would weaken if workers’

Nevertheless, the central challenge in the labour market that impedes the intended outcome lies
in the limited integration between the supply and demand for skills. While education and training
institutions shape the supply of workforce, the types of skills, occupations and jobs demanded
by the economy are determined by the industry. When these two sides are insufficiently aligned,
the labour market may experience persistent skills mismatches, youth unemployment and
underemployment, weak wage progression and a disconnect between productivity and wages.

These indicate that improvements in education and training alone may not translate into better
wage outcomes unless firms simultaneously create high-paying jobs and strengthen demand for
more advanced skills.

Malaysia’s next phase of wage reform should move beyond raising the wage floor towards building
a stronger wage ladder that enables meaningful career progression for workers. While maintaining
an effective national minimum wage remains important for protecting workers at the lower end
of the labour market, wage regulation alone would not transform the underlying structure of

The Role of Government Measures in Cushioning Rising Living Costs
Introduction
As a small and open economy, Malaysia is exposed to heightened global uncertainties, including
volatility in global energy prices. Focusing on the price transmission channel, any disruption could
raise import and production costs, exert upward pressure on consumer prices and, in turn, weigh
on business activities and household spending. Nonetheless, Malaysia’s position as a net energy
exporter provides buffers against the impact in the domestic market. Against this backdrop, this
article examines:
• the impact of higher global oil prices on producer and consumer prices;

and transport-related services that rely on energy and imported inputs. Given the role of Brent

Government Measures to Cushion the Impact of Rising Living Costs
The Government has adopted a broad and complementary set of measures to cushion the impact
of rising living costs and safeguard household wellbeing, particularly during periods of heightened
external cost pressures. These measures operate through two main channels: price stabilisation
measures which help moderate increases in the price of essential goods and services; and
targeted assistance which provides direct financial support to improve the remaining income1 of

eligible households and vulnerable groups. Together, these interventions help preserve households’
purchasing power by addressing both the increase in expenditure and strengthening the financial
capacity to absorb higher living costs.
Price stabilisation measures, particularly capping the prices of RON95 and diesel, help moderate
the transmission of higher global energy prices to the costs of domestic essential items, as
shown in Figure 1.2.4. This is particularly important for lower-income households, which have
smaller income buffers and less capacity to absorb increases in essential expenditure. The price

due to higher global oil and commodity prices. Given that the impact of higher living costs is
heterogeneous across households, the household-level microsimulation indicates that Government
assistance provides additional relative support for lower-income households. Overall, the findings
highlight the complementary nature of the Government’s policy response in safeguarding the
livelihoods of households, particularly during periods of elevated cost pressures. Price stabilisation
measures help contain the increase in household expenditure through the price channel, while

“THE FOURTH MADANI BUDGET:
THE RAKYAT’S BUDGET”

PREAMBLE
Tan Sri Speaker Sir,
I beg to move the Bill intituled “An Act to apply a sum from the
Consolidated Fund for the service of the year 2026 and to
appropriate that sum for the service of that year” be read a
second time.
Bismillahirrahmanirrahim
Assalamualaikum Warahmatullahi Wabarakatuh,
Salam Sejahtera.
Tan Sri Speaker, Honourable Members of this House
and Malaysians whom we serve and cherish,
1. We raise our deepest gratitude to Allah SWT, for it is by His
grace that we gather today to fulfil a solemn trust: to present a Budget
for the coming year. Yet, let it be said clearly – a budget is not merely
a ledger of allocations nor a stack of fiscal tables. It is not a sterile
1

technical document concerned only with deficits and balance sheets.
A budget is a moral testament, a pledge of history and an honest
covenant between a government and its people.
2. As revealed in the Quran:
ن َ وَ ٰخْ ِإ ا ۟ وٓ ُناكَ نَ يرِ ذِ َبمُ لْٱ نَّ ِإ ۝ ارً يذِ بَْت رْ ذِ َبُت لََ وَ لِ يِبسَّ لٱ نَ بْ ٱوَ نَ يكِ سْ مِ لْٱوَ ۥُهَّقحَ ىٰ َبرْ ُقلْٱ اَذ تِ اءَ وَ
۝ ارًًۭوُفكَ ۦهِ ِ برَ لِ نُ ـٰطَ يْ شَّ لٱ نَ اكَ وَ ۖ نِ يطِ ـَٰيشَّ لٱ
“And give the relative his right, and [also] the poor and the
traveller, and do not spend wastefully. Indeed, the wasteful
are brothers of the devils, and ever has Satan been to his Lord
ungrateful.”
(Surah al-Isra’ 17:26-27)
3. The Fourth MADANI Budget rises to meet the demands and
disquiet of our times – grappling with present economic headwinds

(Surah al-Isra’ 17:26-27)
3. The Fourth MADANI Budget rises to meet the demands and
disquiet of our times – grappling with present economic headwinds
while charting a course that averts excess and error. We condemn
the gluttony of those who gorge on debt as though tomorrow did not
exist. We stand firm against leakages and decay. And we refuse the
2

decadence of an entitled elite whose comforts are financed by the
hardship of ordinary citizens. Instead, we choose the steeper, lonelier
road – one of reform, of uncompromising fiscal discipline and of
institutional fortification – for only such a path charts the nation on a
sustainable course.
“Politics should be a noble mirror of our humanity – never
merely calculation or a contest of power.”
Vaclav Havel (poet, thinker and former President of the
Republic of Czech)
4. The world is rattled by tariff wars. The geopolitical order is
coming apart at the seams. The climate is unravelling. And the
furious pace of technological change is upending lives and
livelihoods. In these times, Malaysia can ill afford silence or
complacency. We must dare to shoulder our moment in history, as

is upending lives and
livelihoods. In these times, Malaysia can ill afford silence or
complacency. We must dare to shoulder our moment in history, as
once did the Malaccan empire: cosmopolitan in its laws, respected
for its maritime strength and commerce and admired for its fidelity to
justice. Now it falls on us to prove that a nation modest in geography
can nevertheless be formidable in influence – not through military
3

might, but through moral authority, social equity and the strength of
a just economy.
5. This Budget also opens the first chapter of the Thirteenth
Malaysia Plan (Thirteenth Plan). It is not merely an annual financial

PREFACE
We live in post-normal times, where upheavals strike not in sequence but all at once.
A simultaneity of disruptions that tests nations and societies alike. Geopolitical tensions intensify,
trade frictions multiply, climate breakdown accelerates and financial markets oscillate. Although
recent clarity on the United States tariff policies offers some reprieve, yet the risks of sector-
specific and reciprocal measures still loom and may disrupt the global trading system further and
weigh on growth.
Yet, even in these unsettled times, Malaysia must not choose the path of least resistance. For too
long, our people have called for genuine reform, for a Government that balances external risks
while addressing deep structural impediments at home. This administration embraces that moral

e reform, for a Government that balances external risks
while addressing deep structural impediments at home. This administration embraces that moral
duty. Guided by the Ekonomi MADANI framework, our task is not only to steer the economy on
a steady course, but also restore dignity, uplift the quality of life and ensure progress is shared
fairly among all Malaysians.
While these remain the early days of our reform agenda, yet the results are already apparent.
The economy expanded by 4.4% in the first half of 2025, outpacing many peers equally
burdened by tariff shocks. Growth has been broad-based: households continue to spend with
confidence, investment is rising in both the public and private sectors, tourism activities are

s been broad-based: households continue to spend with
confidence, investment is rising in both the public and private sectors, tourism activities are
booming and construction sites hum with activity. At the same time, the rakyat’s livelihoods are
better protected. Unemployment has recorded the lowest level in a decade, inflation remains
low and the ringgit stands among the region’s most resilient currencies. Even in the face of
a weakened global trading environment, our exporters are adapting and sustaining jobs at
home. On this basis, Malaysia's economy is expected to grow between 4% and 4.8% in 2025 and
4% – 4.5% in 2026.
Budget 2026 is the fourth of the MADANI Budget series and the first under the Thirteenth

d to grow between 4% and 4.8% in 2025 and
4% – 4.5% in 2026.
Budget 2026 is the fourth of the MADANI Budget series and the first under the Thirteenth
Malaysia Plan, 2026 – 2030 (Thirteenth Plan). It marks a passage from reform to transformation,
charting a course where immediate recovery gives way to long-term renewal. The strategic
investments envisioned under the Thirteenth Plan are fully aligned with the twin pillars of
Ekonomi MADANI: 'Raising the Ceiling' of national potential, while 'Raising the Floor' of living
standards. They are designed to catalyse growth, elevate Malaysia’s role in global supply chains
and enhance our human capital. In turn, they will deliver better wages, genuine opportunities for

th, elevate Malaysia’s role in global supply chains
and enhance our human capital. In turn, they will deliver better wages, genuine opportunities for
social mobility and a higher quality of life for the rakyat. With the Thirteenth Plan, Malaysia will
expand its expertise in high growth high value sectors — from artificial intelligence to renewable
energy — positioning our nation at the technological frontier while securing sustainability for
generations to come.

better manage sustainability-related risks and seize new opportunities in the low-carbon economy,

material sustainability risks and opportunities in order to maintain business resilience and competitive
advantage. Hence, large non-listed companies with an annual revenue of RM2 billion and above were
included in the NSRF, due to their wide geographical footprint and exposure to transition risk. As of

limited capacity within enforcement agencies also contribute to challenges in enforcing and
monitoring the minimum wage implementation. Based on the NWCC reports, on average around
9%8 of employers did not adhere to the minimum wage policy.

such as increasing the purchasing power, strengthening safety net for low-wage workers and
maintaining business competitiveness. However, the policy has had minimal impact in increasing
automation adoption and reducing dependency on low-skilled foreign labour, as minimum wage
revisions alone have not made local employment sufficiently attractive, especially in labour-oriented
industries. This underscores the need for a more comprehensive approach, combining wage policy
with broader labour market reforms, to fully realise the aspirations of Ekonomi MADANI framework
and build a more resilient workforce in the future.

Introduction
As a small and highly open economy, Malaysia engages with approximately 90% of countries in
international trade and investment flows. The nation’s firm commitment to liberal and open trade
policies has been a key driver of economic growth, attracting quality investment, generating
employment opportunities and improving household incomes. Malaysia continues to leverage on
the extensive network of trade agreements with major global and regional partners, supported
by a dynamic and resilient economic structure. This outward-oriented approach has resulted in

ents with major global and regional partners, supported
by a dynamic and resilient economic structure. This outward-oriented approach has resulted in
consistently high trade-to-GDP ratio of more than 100% over the years, highlighting the country’s
presence in the global economic landscape. A major advantage of Malaysia’s trade profile is
the diversity of export portfolio, which spans across multiple sectors and product categories.
Strategically located in Southeast Asia, Malaysia maintains strong trade ties with two of the
world’s largest economies, China and the US. Hence, any trade policy change by either country will
significantly impact the global and Malaysia’s economy.

economic policies, trade norms and market access. As one of the world’s largest economies
and trading nation, the US shapes global trade trends through its multinational corporates,
consumption appetite, trade agreement and regulatory frameworks. The re-elected US President
Donald Trump has unveiled a slew of reciprocal tariffs on numerous countries, which have sent
ripples throughout the global economy. The move triggered widespread response, amid geopolitical
tensions, resulting in affected countries reassessing their trade strategies and several imposing

ve triggered widespread response, amid geopolitical
tensions, resulting in affected countries reassessing their trade strategies and several imposing
retaliatory reciprocal tariffs. As such, Malaysia is experiencing both the direct and indirect
repercussions, given the strong linkages in the global supply chain, particularly in the E&E industry.
In light of the changing and challenging trade landscape, Malaysia views this new unfolding
horizon as an opportunity to enhance economic structures while managing the challenges ahead.

While headline inflation on average remains moderate over the years, aggregate figures do not

essential categories such as food & beverages; transport; and housing & utilities.

Conclusion
Price changes affect households differently, reinforcing the need for targeted and data-driven
policy interventions. While headline inflation serves as an important macroeconomic indicator, it
may differ in terms of household-level inflation, particularly for low-income and vulnerable groups.
These households typically allocate a larger share of their budgets for essential goods, such as
food & beverages, health, housing & utilities and transport, with limited room for substitution
when prices rise. Consequently, the impact of household-level inflation is not uniform and can
differ significantly across income groups, locations and household preferences. In this regard,

Introduction
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a suite of technologies that enable machines to exhibit intelligence,
adapt to changing circumstances and amplify human ingenuity and intellectual capabilities. These
technologies encompass a broad spectrum of capabilities including learning, reasoning, problem-
solving and decision-making. Consequently, AI is expected to rapidly reshape technological and
innovation landscapes, while emerging as a critical enabler of progress and inclusive growth.
The adoption of AI is anticipated to enhance competitiveness across socioeconomic activities

as a critical enabler of progress and inclusive growth.
The adoption of AI is anticipated to enhance competitiveness across socioeconomic activities
by enabling businesses to operate more efficiently, creating new opportunities for employment
and contributing to higher living standards. The integration of AI has the potential to contribute
approximately USD115 billion or RM485 billion in value added to the national economy (Ministry
of Digital, 2024). Thus, realising this potential requires not only accelerating adoption but also
ensuring benefits are shared inclusively to prevent the incidence of an AI divide across society.
The Government has set a clear aspiration to become an inclusive and sustainable AI nation

y to prevent the incidence of an AI divide across society.
The Government has set a clear aspiration to become an inclusive and sustainable AI nation
by 2030, as outlined in the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan, 2026 – 2030 (Thirteenth Plan). This is
underpinned by national strategies and frameworks, including the Malaysia Digital Economy
Blueprint, 2021 – 2030; the National Artificial Intelligence Roadmap, 2021 – 2025 (AI-Rmap); the
National Guidelines on AI Governance & Ethics (AIGE) and the Public Sector Artificial Intelligence
(AI) Adaptation Guidelines, as shown in Figure 3.2.1.

assistance to foster closer collaboration among researchers, universities and government research
institutes. Emphasis will also be given to support the protection of intellectual property and drive
homegrown innovations. Furthermore, a more prominent role by the private sector in providing
incubation hubs and sandboxes is critical in bringing AI solutions to market.

Expanding AI-ready datasets and developing national supercomputer facilities will accelerate

expanding rural broadband and community access points. These efforts will enable industry-specific
applications while safeguarding national digital sovereignty.
